lecture_series.title: Balancing the Cost of Utility-Scale Quantum Computing
High Accuracy Simulations with Utility-Scale Quantum Computing

divincenzo_criteria.description: DiVincenzo's 5+2 criteria for physical implementation of quantum computing  used as a hardware-realism overlay on maturity stages.
criteria: Scalable physical system with well-characterized qubits
Long coherence times relative to gate times
(Optional) Interconversion of stationary and flying qubits
divincenzo_criteria.relevance: Applied at Stage C/D to validate hardware-readiness assumptions for advantage claims.

troyer_cost_model.description: Part 6 of the lecture series (2026-04-28): a computation is utility-scale when the value of the problem solved exceeds the cost of solving it. Resource estimation gives the logical qubits; qubit type, fidelity and gate speed give the physical qubits and the runtime; the cost is the runtime times a cost per module-hour that amortizes build and operating cost, illustrated at about $500 to $2,000 per module-hour. Clock speed and modularity dominate: the same chemistry calculation might cost tens of thousands of dollars on a fast, compact machine or millions on a slower or modular one.
troyer_cost_model.note: The evaluator's cost panel prices today's devices per shot and does not yet apply this model.

proven_speedup.label: Proven Speedup
proven_speedup.description: Algorithms with a proven asymptotic speedup over the best known classical algorithm. A proof is not a practical advantage: quadratic speedups (amplitude estimation, Grover) are unlikely to survive error-correction overhead, and HHL's exponential speedup assumes efficient loading and readout of the data. Only Shor's superpolynomial speedup survives the screen here.

problems.speedup: Quadratic: O(1/ε) vs classical O(1/ε²)
problems.troyer_assessment: QAE provides provable quadratic speedup for amplitude estimation. However, the constant-factor overhead of error correction means utility requires problems with ε < 10⁻⁴ where the quadratic advantage overcomes QEC cost.
problems.utility_threshold: Requires ~10⁶ logical operations to beat classical; current toy instance has ~40 logical qubits

problems.speedup: Superpolynomial: O(n³) vs sub-exponential classical (GNFS)
problems.troyer_assessment: Shor's algorithm is the canonical example of superpolynomial quantum speedup. Utility requires factoring 2048+ bit integers  our 4-bit toy instance demonstrates the algorithm but is far from utility scale.
problems.utility_threshold: RSA-2048: about 1,400 logical qubits and 6.5 billion Toffoli gates, under a million noisy qubits for under a week at a 0.1% gate error rate (Gidney 2025, arXiv:2505.15917), down from 20 million noisy qubits for 8 hours (Gidney and Ekerå 2019, arXiv:1905.09749)

problems.speedup: Quadratic: O(√N) vs classical O(N), provably optimal (BBBV)
problems.troyer_assessment: Grover's quadratic speedup is provably optimal but only halves the effective key length, and only if its iterations run in series. NIST expects Grover to give little or no advantage against AES and considers AES-128 secure for decades to come (NIST PQC FAQ); NSA's CNSA 2.0, as CNSA 1.0 did, still requires AES-256 for US national security systems. The practical threat is from Shor, not Grover.
problems.utility_threshold: AES-128 search needs about 2⁶⁴ Grover iterations in series: about 2⁸⁶ T gates on 2,953 logical qubits with a reversible AES oracle (Grassl et al., arXiv:1512.04965)

problems.speedup: Quadratic: O(√N) vs classical O(N), provably optimal
problems.troyer_assessment: Provably optimal quadratic speedup, but the QRAM assumption for data loading is critical. Without efficient QRAM, the speedup may be negated by data-access overhead.
problems.utility_threshold: Requires N > 10⁶ with efficient oracle; current 4-qubit instance is far below

problems.speedup: Exponential: O(polylog(N)) vs classical O(N·κ) for sparse systems
problems.troyer_assessment: HHL offers exponential speedup but with critical caveats: (1) requires efficient state preparation, (2) only provides quantum state output (readout bottleneck), (3) condition number κ must be polylog(N). Practical utility requires all three conditions simultaneously.
problems.utility_threshold: Utility requires N > 10⁶ with κ = O(polylog N) and efficient I/O

problems.algorithm: Direct sampling of a loss probability (planned: amplitude estimation)
problems.speedup: None as implemented; quadratic at best for the planned amplitude estimation
problems.troyer_assessment: The kernel samples the probability of marked states directly, which has the same 1/√shots error as classical Monte Carlo; it never implemented amplitude estimation. Amplitude estimation of a loss probability would inherit the quadratic speedup of problem 03 and its limits: error-correction overhead and loading the distribution outweigh it.

problems.speedup: Exponential (same HHL caveats)
problems.troyer_assessment: Climate PDEs are well-suited to HHL if the state preparation and readout problems can be solved. The exponential speedup applies to the linear algebra core but practical utility requires end-to-end advantage including I/O.

heuristic_potential.label: Heuristic / Unproven Advantage
heuristic_potential.description: Variational and approximate algorithms without proven speedup over classical. These rely on empirical performance that may or may not survive scaling. Troyer emphasizes these are the highest-risk category for utility claims.
heuristic_potential.note: Five problems originally in this category (01_hubbard, 02_catalysis, 07_drug_discovery, 14_materials_discovery, 17_nuclear_physics) were upgraded from VQE to QPE and reclassified to simulation_native. Their QPE implementations target naturally quantum Hamiltonians, where QPE is exponentially cheaper than exact diagonalization once a state that overlaps the ground state well has been prepared; no advantage over the best classical methods is established.

problems.speedup: None proven; on bounded-degree graphs, constant-depth expectation values are classically computable
problems.troyer_assessment: No proven quantum advantage for QAOA on MaxCut. The Goemans-Williamson algorithm achieves a 0.878 approximation in polynomial time and outperforms QAOA at any constant depth on certain instances (Bravyi et al., arXiv:1910.08980). On bounded-degree graphs the expected cut of constant-depth QAOA can be computed classically, although sampling its output can be classically hard even at depth one (Farhi and Harrow, arXiv:1602.07674). Whether higher-depth QAOA offers an advantage is open.
problems.archival_reason: No proven speedup; no QAOA is known to beat Goemans-Williamson

problems.speedup: None proven
problems.troyer_assessment: Classical protein folding has been revolutionized by AI (AlphaFold). QAOA for lattice protein models has no proven advantage. The quantum approach would need to handle realistic all-atom models to compete.

problems.speedup: Exponential in specific cases (kernel evaluation)
problems.troyer_assessment: QML speedups depend on data encoding assumptions. If classical data must be loaded into quantum states, the loading cost often negates the kernel speedup. Proven advantages exist only for specific, contrived problem structures.

problems.speedup: None proven
problems.troyer_assessment: Same QAOA limitations as MaxCut. Classical scheduling algorithms are highly optimized for industrial use. No proven quantum advantage for combinatorial optimization at any depth.

problems.speedup: None proven
problems.troyer_assessment: Trajectory optimization is well-served by classical methods. QAOA for routing/scheduling has the same unproven-advantage limitations as other combinatorial optimization problems.

simulation_native.label: Quantum Simulation (Native Advantage Potential)
simulation_native.description: Problems where the quantum system being simulated IS quantum  Feynman's original motivation. These have the strongest theoretical case for utility and require fault-tolerant hardware; even so, no generic exponential advantage has been established for ground-state chemistry (Lee et al., Nat. Commun. 14, 1952, 2023). The category also holds the QEC repetition code, as infrastructure. Includes problems upgraded from VQE to QPE that target naturally quantum Hamiltonians.

problems.speedup: Exponential over exact diagonalization if the initial state overlaps the ground state well; not established against the best classical methods
problems.troyer_assessment: Upgraded to QPE for Hubbard Hamiltonians, naturally quantum systems that tensor-network methods find hard in two dimensions. Once a state with good ground-state overlap is prepared, QPE's cost is polynomial, exponentially below exact diagonalization; whether such states are cheap to prepare for large 2D lattices, and whether QPE then beats DMRG and quantum Monte Carlo, is open. Our 2-site instance is pedagogical; utility would need 2D lattices wider than DMRG can treat.
problems.upgrade_note: VQE→QPE (April 2026). Reclassified from heuristic_potential to simulation_native.

problems.speedup: Exponential over full configuration interaction if the initial state overlaps the ground state well; not established against the best classical methods
problems.troyer_assessment: Upgraded to QPE for molecular Hamiltonians. Hoefler, Häner and Troyer see 'a huge potential in material science and chemistry'. QPE is exponentially cheaper than FCI once a state with good ground-state overlap is prepared, but coupled cluster, DMRG and selected CI already treat many large molecules accurately, and no generic exponential advantage over them has been established (Lee et al., Nat. Commun. 14, 1952, 2023). The case rests on strongly correlated systems such as FeMoco. The current H₂ instance is pedagogical.
problems.upgrade_note: VQE→QPE (April 2026). Reclassified from heuristic_potential to simulation_native.

problems.speedup: Exponential over exact diagonalization if the initial state overlaps the ground state well; not established against the best classical methods
problems.troyer_assessment: Upgraded to QPE for molecular binding energy Hamiltonians. A quantum advantage in drug discovery would need strongly correlated electronic structure, such as some transition states and metal-containing active sites, that DFT and coupled cluster cannot treat reliably, and QPE is a candidate there only if a state with good ground-state overlap can be prepared. Our instance is a labelled toy model.
problems.upgrade_note: VQE→QPE (April 2026). Reclassified from heuristic_potential to simulation_native.

problems.speedup: Exponential over exact diagonalization if the initial states overlap the target states well; not established against the best classical methods
problems.troyer_assessment: Upgraded to QPE for strongly-correlated materials (e.g., high-Tc superconductors), where DFT is unreliable. Simulating the dynamics of correlated electrons is believed to be classically hard in general, but for ground-state and gap estimation QPE's advantage depends on preparing states that overlap the target states well. Our instance is a labelled toy model.
problems.upgrade_note: VQE→QPE (April 2026). Reclassified from heuristic_potential to simulation_native.

problems.speedup: N/A  infrastructure, not application
problems.troyer_assessment: QEC is enabling infrastructure, not an application. The repetition code demonstrates error detection but is not a path to utility. Surface codes and beyond are needed for fault-tolerant computation. See errorcorrectionzoo.org for comprehensive code taxonomy.

problems.speedup: Exponential over exact diagonalization if the initial state overlaps the ground state well; not established against the best classical methods
problems.troyer_assessment: Upgraded to QPE for a nuclear EFT Hamiltonian, the deuteron model of Dumitrescu et al. (PRL 120, 210501, 2018). A quantum advantage would need heavier nuclei, where shell-model truncation becomes severe, and QPE is a candidate there only if a state with good ground-state overlap can be prepared.
problems.upgrade_note: VQE→QPE (April 2026). Reclassified from heuristic_potential to simulation_native.

problems.speedup: Potential exponential for transport simulation; not established
problems.troyer_assessment: Exciton transport in photosynthetic systems is inherently quantum, but the open-system dynamics of light-harvesting complexes of the size studied so far are routinely simulated classically, with hierarchical equations of motion or Lindblad master equations. An advantage would need systems large and strongly coupled enough to defeat those methods.

problems.algorithm: Trotterized spin chain (stand-in for lattice gauge dynamics)
problems.speedup: Exponential for real-time dynamics of interacting gauge theories (sign problem); none for this kernel, a classically solvable Ising chain
problems.classical_best: Lattice QCD (Euclidean, limited to static properties)
problems.troyer_assessment: Lattice gauge theory is arguably the strongest utility candidate. Classical lattice QCD cannot simulate real-time dynamics due to the sign problem. Quantum simulation of gauge theories could enable predictions impossible classically, but realistic lattice sizes need large fault-tolerant machines (Kan and Nam, arXiv:2107.12769, give the gate costs). This project's kernel is not yet such a simulation: it evolves a transverse-field Ising chain, which has no gauge fields and maps to free fermions.

summary.key_insight: 7/20 problems target algorithms with a proven asymptotic speedup (QAE x2, Grover x2, HHL x2, Shor), though 06's kernel samples its loss probability directly and never implemented amplitude estimation; six of the seven are archived, because the quadratic speedups do not survive error-correction overhead and HHL's depends on data loading, leaving only Shor's superpolynomial speedup active. 5/20 rely on heuristics with no proven speedup (QAOA x4, swap test), all archived. 8/20 sit in the simulation category: seven quantum simulation problems (five upgraded from VQE to QPE) and the QEC repetition code as infrastructure. 9 problems are active and 11 archived.
summary.divincenzo_note: DiVincenzo's criteria (scalable qubits, initialization, coherence, universal gates, measurement) are applied as a hardware-realism overlay at Stage C/D. Current quantum hardware challenges  limited qubit counts, short coherence times, high error rates  map directly to DiVincenzo gaps that must close before utility-scale advantage is achievable.
